text: Plenty of organizations stand up something called a Cloud Center of Excellence and get a group that reviews architecture proposals and approves or rejects them — essentially a gate, in the last lesson's terms, wearing a more ambitious name. That provokes exactly the shadow-IT response we just covered: teams learn that going to the CCoE means waiting, so they avoid it. A group whose entire function is reviewing other people's work isn't a center of excellence in any real sense — it hasn't built anything an excellent team could point to and use.

A functioning CCoE is a platform team, and platform teams own things. It owns the shared module catalog from course 8 — the landing zone network module, the storage module with encryption and logging already wired in — built, versioned, and maintained centrally. A product team that needs a storage account consumes that module instead of designing one from scratch and submitting it for review. It already satisfies the policy baseline by construction: compliance by default, not compliance by checklist.

The CCoE also owns the policy baseline itself — the Azure Policy initiatives and AWS SCPs from Lesson 17, the tagging enforcement from Lesson 18 — maintained and versioned the way any team owns the code it ships. And it owns the landing zone foundation, the management group structure and account vending, keeping it correct as the organization's needs change.

None of that pays off if teams don't know it exists. A CCoE that builds excellent modules but never runs onboarding, never documents how to consume them, has only done half the job — teams keep reinventing what already exists because they didn't know to look. Real CCoE output includes office hours and documentation that gets a new team from needing a subscription to being deployed and compliant without asking a platform engineer to do it by hand.

The honest test: ask a product team whether, last quarter, they consumed something the CCoE built, or waited for the CCoE to approve something they built themselves. The first answer means the CCoE is doing its job. The second means it's a review committee with a better title — and the fix isn't more people on the committee, it's shifting its time from reviewing proposals to building the modules that make most proposals unnecessary.
